name: Shelter folk
one_line: The one house nobody had to build: an overhang, a hearth in the same spot for ten thousand years, and hands on the ceiling.

needs: an overhang, a recess at a cliff foot, or a cave mouth: a roof nobody built, with a dry floor above the flood and back from the drip line
a spring, seep or stream within a short walk

staples: game from the valley below (deer, ibex, antelope, wallaby by biome)
nuts in season: acorn, hazel, pinyon, marula by biome
roots and tubers dug with a stick
eggs, grubs, snails, honey when found
how: the spear, from a lookout the roof gives for free
snares on the game trails below the cliff
gathering by season within a day's walk, then the next overhang
preserve: strips smoked over the hearth (the smoke leaves under the lip) or dried on the sun-side rock
nuts cached in a pit at the back wall

fuel.note: whatever the land outside gives, dragged up: dead branch from the woods, brush from the scrub, dung on the savanna; small fires, set back from the drip line so the smoke rolls out under the lip

shelter.form: nothing built: the overhang is the roof; a hide screen or a low stacked-stone wall along the drip line closes the mouth; the hearth back from the lip; beds of grass and brush on the dry floor at the back

CAVES.fuel: branch dragged in from whatever grows at the mouth; a shelter burns small
CAVES.food: what the valley outside gives; game taken at the entrance
CAVES.shelter: the cave mouth itself: the hearth at the daylight line, never deeper; the dark at the back is left alone
CAVES.palette: limestone grey, soot black, hearth orange on the ceiling

CANYON.fuel: juniper and pinyon branch from the rim, cottonwood from the floor, dung
CANYON.food: pinyon nuts, agave hearts pit-roasted, bighorn, cactus fruit
CANYON.shelter: an alcove in the sandstone wall, sun-warmed in winter, shaded in summer; a stacked-stone wall at the lip
CANYON.palette: red sandstone, ochre bands, cottonwood gold, desert-varnish black

TEMPERATE_DECIDUOUS.fuel: oak and beech branch, hazel brush
TEMPERATE_DECIDUOUS.food: acorns and hazelnuts, deer, the river's fish in the valley
TEMPERATE_DECIDUOUS.shelter: a limestone cliff-foot abri above a river bend, hide screens against the north wind; the classic
TEMPERATE_DECIDUOUS.palette: limestone cream, oak brown, moss green, ochre red

MEDITERRANEAN_SCRUB.food: holm-oak acorns, ibex and rabbit, wild olive, snails after rain
MEDITERRANEAN_SCRUB.shelter: a valley-facing overhang in limestone, cool in the summer heat; a brush screen
MEDITERRANEAN_SCRUB.palette: pale limestone, sage grey-green, terracotta ochre, hard blue shade

SAVANNA.fuel: acacia branch, dung, dry grass to catch
SAVANNA.food: antelope, tubers, baobab and marula fruit, honey, flying termites in season
SAVANNA.shelter: the overhang of a granite kopje or a sandstone escarpment; the shade is the point; a thorn fence at the lip
SAVANNA.palette: granite grey, red laterite ochre, dry-grass gold

TROPICAL_DRY_FOREST.food: deer and wild pig, wild yams, fruit in the wet season, palm hearts
TROPICAL_DRY_FOREST.shelter: a limestone overhang lived in through the dry months, the floor swept; a leaf screen in the rains
TROPICAL_DRY_FOREST.palette: bleached grey trunks, red-peeling bark, ochre red, dust

TEPUI.fuel: scant: stunted Bonnetia branch and shrub brush from the clefts; every fire is small and precious
TEPUI.food: little on the summit: a waystation, fed from the slope forest below; frogs and what the clefts give
TEPUI.shelter: a recess in the black-crusted quartzite out of the cloud-wind; the cosiest ceiling in the game because outside it never stops raining
TEPUI.palette: black quartzite, white summit sand, cloud grey, sundew red

knows: nettles at the drip line: greens in spring, fibre in autumn
tinder fungus and punk wood, the ember carrier's heart
the fat-bearing nuts by biome (acorn, hazel, pinyon, marula) and how to leach the bitter ones
aromatic leaves laid in the bedding to keep the biting insects down
plantkeeper.teaches_flavour: why nettles crowd the drip line and nothing grows under the roof; how the ash under the hearth tells the years like tree rings
plantkeeper.teaches_practical: leach acorns in the stream before you eat them; punk wood holds a coal, green wood kills one

techniques.name: Ochre
techniques.verb: grind red and yellow iron earth on a stone, mix it with fat
techniques.teaches: practical long before it was art: sunscreen, insect repellent, the cure rubbed into hide; then a hand pressed to the wall and the paint blown round it, the oldest signature there is. It is the player's own mark on the world, laid beside the forgotten waymarks
techniques.unlocks: paint: mark your own trail on rock and tree beside the old waymarks; ochre in the store lets the maker cure hide

techniques.name: Ember carrier
techniques.verb: wrap a live coal in tinder fungus or punk wood and bark
techniques.teaches: fire is never made, only carried; a shelter people's whole life is carrying it from one overhang to the next (the Iceman carried his in maple leaves in a birch-bark box)
techniques.unlocks: carry fire for a day or more with no light; lay a new fire from it; it goes cold if neglected

techniques.name: Knapping
techniques.verb: strike flakes off flint, chert or obsidian at the mouth of the shelter
techniques.teaches: the edge is in the stone already; you take away what is not knife. The floor of flakes outlasts everything else you own
techniques.unlocks: a knife: dress carcasses, cut cordage; the knapping floor glitters for ten thousand years

techniques.name: Hide
techniques.verb: scrape the flesh side on a beam, smoke it over the hearth, rub in fat and ochre, sew with sinew and a bone needle
techniques.teaches: every warm thing the player could wear began here; smoke and ochre are what keep a skin from rotting
techniques.unlocks: the maker turns hide into cloaks, bags and shelter skins; the camp's shelter ceiling

ladder: the hearth under a roof nobody built
forage: game, nuts and roots within a day's walk
smoke over the hearth; a nut cache at the back wall
hide and ochre go out on the road; the shelter grows no further
growth.restraint: the camp is small because the roof is: it takes what a day's walk regrows, and when the near woods thin it moves to the next overhang and comes back in a few years. The same shelters were lived in for tens of thousands of years by never being over-lived
growth.ceiling_hint: a shelter camp stays a handful: no fundamental, no village, the floor of the ladder and honestly so; what it has instead is the oldest fire in the world, still lit

signatures.what: hands and animals in red and yellow on the ceiling and back wall, under soot and moss
signatures.restore: cleared: a camp scrubs the soot back and the hands come out; a restored camp paints its own beside them
signatures.inherits: the waymark is already on the wall: the site reads as a shelter from across the valley

signatures.what: a metre of layered ash and charcoal under the hearth spot, every band a generation
signatures.restore: cleared: the new fire is laid on the old ash in the same spot
signatures.inherits: a dry, drained hearth floor; the fire lights first time

signatures.what: a scatter of flakes and spent cores glittering at the mouth
signatures.restore: restored: the knapper works the same spot
signatures.inherits: good stone already sorted; the knapper starts from the first day

signatures.what: a slab with a worn hollow, red in the grain
signatures.restore: restored: set upright by the hearth and ground on again
signatures.inherits: ochre from the first day; the maker's paint and hide cure

signatures.what: a tumbled line of stacked stone along the drip line at the mouth
signatures.restore: restored: the camp restacks it and the mouth is closed against the wind
signatures.inherits: a windbreak; the shelter ceiling from the first night

ruin.plants_differ: nettle, goosefoot and elder crowd the drip line and the old ash, rich with bone and charcoal; nothing grows under the roof itself, and the dry floor stays bare for ten thousand years

aesthetic.silhouette: a lit mouth in a cliff: the hearth glow on the ceiling, the only fire in the game that lights stone instead of sky, the cosiest light there is; a hide screen and a low wall at the lip; figures against the orange
sounds: the fire's crackle echoing off the roof
wind that stops at the mouth
props: the hearth in its ash pit
a hide stretched on a frame

huts.workshop_form: a lean-to of hide screen and low stacked stone built against the back wall under the overhang, the roof nobody built over it, the ochre hands on the rock above and the hearth glow on its hides
soft: a hide pegged on a frame, flesh side out
hanks of sinew hung from a rock knob
nettle stalks soaking in a hollow, fibre being twisted from them
a cloak half sewn with a bone needle
hard: a knapping floor of flint flakes at the mouth
a grinding slab with a red hollow and a lump of ochre
bone needles in a row on a flat stone
a hammerstone and a spent core
hearth: the hearth in its ash pit, set back from the drip line
a rack of smoked strips over the coals
hot stones in a hide-lined pit
an ember bundle in bark by the fire
huts.porch_sign: a hide stretched on a frame at the lip, red hands pressed on the rock above it
huts.library: a dry recess at the back wall beside the nut cache; the winter-count is painted on a hide stretched on a frame, beside the old hands on the stone
third_places: the lip of the overhang looking out over the valley

real_world.region: southern Cape coast, South Africa, c. 100,000 years ago
real_world.note: two abalone shells holding red paint: ochre ground on quartzite slabs, mixed with heated crushed bone, charcoal and a liquid, the oldest known paint-making kit; engraved ochre from the same cave is c. 75,000 years old

real_world.analogue: Hand stencils: Maros-Pangkep karst (Sulawesi) and El Castillo (Cantabria)
real_world.region: Indonesia and Spain, c. 37,000–51,000 years ago
real_world.note: red-ochre hand stencils at Leang Timpuseng at least 39,900 years old, a warty pig at Leang Tedongnge at least 45,500, a hunting scene at Leang Karampuang c. 51,200; at El Castillo a red disk c. 40,800 and hand stencils c. 37,300, Europe's oldest dated paintings, in a cave mouth lived in from the Proto-Aurignacian to the Bronze Age; all dated by uranium-series on the calcite over the paint

real_world.analogue: The Dordogne abris (Abri Pataud, Laugerie, Cro-Magnon)
real_world.region: Vézère valley, France, c. 35,000–20,000 years ago
real_world.note: limestone cliff-foot shelters above a river; Abri Pataud at Les Eyzies holds 15,000 years of layers, Aurignacian to Solutrean, hearths, burials and some two million finds; the Cro-Magnon shelter next door gave its name to us all in 1868

real_world.region: Madhya Pradesh, India, Acheulean to medieval
real_world.note: more than 750 sandstone shelters, some 400 painted in red hematite, manganese black and charcoal; lived in from the Lower Palaeolithic, painted from the Mesolithic (c. 10,000 BCE) into historic times; UNESCO 2003

real_world.region: Mirarr country, Arnhem Land and Kakadu, northern Australia, 65,000 years to now
real_world.note: Madjedbebe shelter occupied 65,000 ± 6,000 years ago (at least 50,000), ground ochre and grinding stones in its lowest levels; the Ubirr galleries nearby painted and repainted over millennia, most of what shows c. 2,000 years old, x-ray fish and a thylacine

red ochre ground and mixed with butterfat, perfumed with Commiphora resin, worn on skin and hair: ochre-and-butter mixes of this kind test at SPF 3.5–10.7 on skin, and it is used where water is scarce because it flakes off with the dirt; also said to keep mosquitoes off

real_world.analogue: Mesa Verde cliff dwellings (a note, not this people)
real_world.note: Ancestral Puebloan farmers built more than 600 stone villages into sandstone alcoves; a shelter site lived by canyon and desert folk with a crop, not by foragers: the same roof, a different life
